title: Hepadnavirus tropism determined by diversified NTCP functionality in Feline species
summary: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) exhibits a narrow host range, largely determined by sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptides (NTCP), a hepatic bile acid transporter acting as the HBV receptor. NTCP among animals appears to have evolved following trade-off mutations to lose its viral receptor activity while preserving its transporter function. Here, through profiling of the NTCP homologs from 23 mammalian species, we uncover unexpected functional heterogeneity of feline NTCPs. NTCPs derived from cat, tiger, and leopard supported viral preS1 binding and HBV infection, whereas lion-NTCP was deficient for preS1 binding and, notably, exhibited markedly reduced bile acid transport. Cat-NTCP was further demonstrated to have viral receptor function by productive infection in primary cat hepatocytes. Experimental mutagenesis identified double substitution at positions 191 and 268 as key determinants: introducing lion-type substitutions into cat-NTCP (G191R and T268A) abolished preS1 binding, whereas reciprocal substitutions in lion-NTCP restored receptor function. Molecular dynamics simulations suggested that lion-NTCP adopts conformation in which a transmembrane helix bending enlarges the whole bile acid tunnel and disrupts preS1 compatibility. Such differences also determined host susceptibility to another feline-infected domestic cat HBV. These findings reveal diversified NTCP functionality with evolutionary plasticity that acquires resistance to hepadnavirus infection at the expense of physiological transporter function.

title: Distinct binding modes shape exploitable asymmetries between echinocandin and triterpenoid resistance landscapes in Fks1
summary: Echinocandins are the first-line treatment for invasive fungal infections and work by inhibiting the fungal {beta}-1,3-glucan synthase Fks1. Recently, a first-in-class triterpenoid Fks1 inhibitor, ibrexafungerp, was approved for clinical use. The extent to which the difference between these drug classes alters the landscape of resistance mutations in Fks1 is unknown. We used deep mutational scanning (DMS) to quantify the effects of all single-amino-acid variants spanning 159 residues across the three canonical Fks1 resistance hotspots and flanking regions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Drug selections revealed widespread position-specific cross-resistance and differential resistance, including an ibrexafungerp-specific resistance cluster downstream of hotspot 2 that defines a novel triterpenoid-specific resistance hotspot. We defined this as hotspot 4 and redefined the boundaries of the remaining three canonical echinocandin hotspots, based on the mutational landscape of our DMS analyses. Susceptibility testing of individual FKS1 variants of S. cerevisiae and Candidozyma auris strains confirmed conserved class-specific and cross-resistance patterns. Structure-guided ligand placement, molecular dynamics-based simulated annealing, and DMS-informed pose selection linked drug-specific phenotypes to distinct interaction networks, providing a molecular rationale for the observed differential resistance patterns. These data provide a framework for predicting antifungal resistance, informing treatment strategies and future drug design.

title: Differential properties of gp120 from HIV-1 group M subtypes A and B
summary: HIV-1 group M subtypes A and B differ substantially in their gp120 sequence. To determine whether these differences contribute to subtype-specific complications, particularly pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), rats were injected with gp120 from subtype A or B. Pulmonary artery (PA) remodeling was assessed after four weeks using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and the Vessel Morphometry Analysis tool by Autona (autona.org). Subtype A gp120 potently increased PA wall thickness and right ventricular hypertrophy. The CD4-binding region of subtype A lacks a stretch of 16 amino acids (V1 N-glycosylation site), and experiments showed stronger binding of subtype B to CD4. Subtype B gp120 contains an RGKV sequence, which resembles the RGKR sequence of the rabies virus glycoprotein G that binds to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR). Subtype A gp120 possesses a KDKK sequence instead. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that both sites are surface-exposed. Although nAChR is expressed in PA cells and could potentially drive the pronounced effects of subtype A, MD simulations estimated that subtype B gp120 binds more strongly to nAChR. We also noted a single amino acid difference immediately preceding the REKR furin cleavage sequence: glutamate in subtype A versus glutamine in subtype B gp120. Simulations predicted that subtype A gp120 interacts more effectively with furin, and enzyme assays demonstrated that subtype A promotes a positive feedback loop more strongly than subtype B. Thus, HIV-1 gp120 subtype A is more potent in promoting PAH, and the mechanism may involve enhancing furin activity to elevate gp120 levels.

title: Uncovering Features of ProteinMPNN with Sparse Autoencoders
summary: Customization and modification of machine learning derived sequences can be achieved by understanding the mechanics behind state-of-the-art protein design models such as ProteinMPNN. Uninterpretability is hypothesized to be due largely to polysemanticity where neural networks store more features than they have dimensions. Here, we introduce sparse autoencoders (SAEs) into ProteinMPNN which expand its latent space and uncovers correlations between the activations in sparse dimensions and the presence of protein features such as secondary structure, residue volume, residue shape, disulfide bridges, and coordination to ligands. Additionally, we show that sparse activations can be manipulated to produce a variant of the short chain variable fragment Brolucizumab that is more thermostable than variants produced by traditional machine learning methods based on high temperature molecular dynamics simulations. Thus, SAEs provide both mechanistic understanding of protein design models and allow customizable manipulation of sequence prediction.

title: RawMod: Modification-Agnostic Detection of DNA Base Modifications from Nanopore Signal Pileups
summary: Summary: Identifying epigenetically modified bases (e.g., methylation) is crucial for many important applications such as discovering mechanisms of cancer development, cell differentiation, and bacterial defense. Nanopore sequencing generates electrical signals that can differentiate canonical bases from modified ones. To detect base modifications from signals, machine learning (ML) methods and statistical approaches are commonly used. These methods can either detect a specific modification type or require an additional unmodified copy of the same DNA as a control group. However, no released model detects modification types beyond those it was trained for, which makes it difficult to detect rare modification types without an unmodified control. Our goal is to accurately identify the presence of modified sites regardless of their modification type, which we define as modification-agnostic detection. To this end, we propose RawMod, a transformer-based modification-agnostic and control-free method for detecting epigenetically modified genomic positions. The key idea of RawMod is to compare the raw signals of many reads at each site with the unmodified reference sequence, using a small model that learns many modification types as a single modified class. Based on our extensive evaluations on the detection of various modification types (5mC, 5hmC, 4mC, 6mA, and 5hmU) using various genomes, RawMod achieves the highest mean AUROC across modifications compared to control-based methods and control-free modification models. A single RawMod model with 0.23M parameters detects five modification types with a mean AUROC of 0.964, against 0.799 for the best released model. When a modification type is withheld from training, RawMod still detects it (AUROC 0.91--0.98), provided another modification of the same base was seen in training. We use RawMod to map 5hmU without a control across a 7.7 Mb contig of the Amphidinium carterae genome, consistent with two published trends. Further, we show that the modification-aware embeddings from RawMod can be used to differentiate read origin (e.g., cell types, tumor/normal origin, and native/PCR-amplified DNA). We discuss how RawMod can enable further work on label-free classification of cell types using these modification-aware embeddings. Availability and Implementation: RawMod is available at https://github.com/STORMgroup/RawMod and at https://huggingface.co/STORMResearch/RawMod. We also provide the scripts to fully reproduce our results on our GitHub page and release our datasets on SquiDBase.

title: BIG-TB: A benchmark for evaluating prediction and interpretability of sequence-based machine learning using Mycobacterium tuberculosis  genomes
summary: Foundation models aim to learn useful representations of biological sequences, but are hindered by a lack of benchmarks to jointly evaluate predictive performance and variant attribution on diverse tasks. To this end, we present the Benchmark for Interpretable prediction from Genomes of Tuberculosis, BIG-TB. We curate over 17,000 genomes with high-quality sequencing data and experimentally measured antibiotic resistance phenotypes, combined with a curated list of WHO-catalogue of resistance-associated variants, and provide these data in an ML-ready format. BIG-TB defines two tasks: (1) predictive performance of antibiotic resistance phenotypes, and (2) attribution of predictions to known resistance-conferring variants. Using our tasks, we evaluate DNA- and protein-based foundation models, showing that DNA-based foundation models do not yet outperform simple machine learning baselines (mean test AUC = 0.888 vs. 0.865 for best CNN variant vs. best Evo2 variant across drugs). In a lineage-informed evaluation across DNA and protein modalities, predictive signal for well-characterized drugs was largely preserved (mean AUC 0.846-0.963). Across both evaluation settings, models with the highest predictive performance did not necessarily achieve the strongest recovery of resistance variants, underscoring the value of evaluating both predictive accuracy and biological interpretability. Overall, BIG-TB provides a reusable resource for developing sequence representations that are both accurate and mechanistically meaningful.

title: Evolution of herbicide resistance through co-option of an ethylene-associated nitrilase
summary: Adaptive evolution frequently proceeds through the co-option of pre-existing biological functions, yet the molecular mechanisms by which such co-option generates new adaptive traits over contemporary evolutionary timescales remain poorly understood. Herbicide-resistant weeds provide a powerful model for addressing this question because enhanced herbicide metabolism has repeatedly evolved within only a few decades. Here, we show that resistance to cyhalofop-butyl in Echinochloa crus-galli evolved through the co-option of EcNIT4A2, which encodes a nitrilase that normally functions in ethylene-associated cyanide detoxification. Genetic mapping, transcriptomics and transgenic analyses identified EcNIT4A2 as the major determinant of resistance. A D317G substitution enhanced its herbicide-detoxifying activity. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that this substitution facilitates substrate access to the catalytic pocket. A promoter structural variant markedly increased EcNIT4A2 expression. Our findings reveal how coding and regulatory changes can jointly drive the co-option and optimization of a conserved metabolic function during rapid adaptation under intense anthropogenic selection.

title: Comparative cryo-EM structures of CGMMV and ToMMV reveal divergent coat protein packing and electrostatics indicating Tobamovirus host specificity
summary: Tobamoviruses are a group of economically important plant viruses exhibiting extreme stability and persistence. Despite high morphological similarity, they show extensive host-family specificity, induce a wide range of symptoms, and inflict significant global yield losses in fruit and vegetable crops. Composed of a rod-shaped helical assembly of identical coat proteins encasing a single-stranded RNA, tobamoviruses have long served as fundamental models for understanding helical assemblies. Here we report the cryo-EM structures of two viruses from this genus, cucumber green mottle mosaic virus (CGMMV) and tomato mottle mosaic virus (ToMMV), at 2.86 [A] and 2.71 [A] resolution, respectively, revealing divergent packing strategies within the virion assembly. Whereas the solanaceous-infecting ToMMV closely mirrors genetically-similar canonical tobacco mosaic virus (TMV), CGMMV employs a specialized hydrophobic packing strategy based at the solvent-exposed inner loop lining the solvent-exposed central canal. Comparative biophysical and molecular dynamics analyses from the reconstructed structures reveal more stable and compact protein packing for CGMMV at both the subunit and assembly levels. Furthermore, we identify a conserved electrostatic pentapeptide motif (residues 113 to117) on the lower radial alpha helix that serves as an additional RNA-stabilizing region, harbouring a clade-defining Lys113 synapomorphy in cucurbit-infecting tobamoviruses. Together, our findings elucidate how subtle electrostatic tuning and divergent hydrophobic packing strategies drive differential virion stability and host-family adaptation within a strictly conserved helical scaffold.

title: Substrate binding and activation mechanism of the essential bacterial septal cell wall synthase FtsW
summary: Septal peptidoglycan (sPG) synthesis in most bacteria is driven by the essential, highly conserved FtsWIQLB synthase complex, comprising the SEDS (Shape, Elongation, Division, and Sporulation) glycosyltransferase FtsW, the monofunctional transpeptidase FtsI, and the scaffolding and regulatory subcomplex FtsQLB. Although apo structures of FtsWIQLB are known, no substrate-bound structures exist, likely due to the intrinsic flexibility of lipid II (L2) substrates. Here, we combined all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of E. coli FtsWIQLB with cysteine-based mutagenesis and cell-based assays to investigate donor and acceptor L2 binding sites in FtsW and to elucidate the complex's activation mechanism. We show that conserved arginine residues adjacent to membrane-accessible cavities in FtsW coordinate donor and acceptor L2 pyrophosphate groups, stabilizing substrate binding. The FtsWIQLB complex appears to adopt a self-inhibitory architecture in which gating elements and a periplasmic loop prevent the donor and acceptor from approaching FtsW's catalytic residue D297. Activation by FtsN or a superfission FtsW variant relieves these constraints, stabilizes acceptor-site binding, and reorients both substrates into a catalytically primed state. Long donor glycan chains further stabilize this activated conformation at the acceptor site, possibly promoting processive sPG polymerization. Comparative modeling of ESKAPE pathogen homologs reveals both conserved and divergent features of binding-site engagement and activation. We corroborate these computational findings with cysteine-based mutagenesis and crosslinking experiments. These results establish a mechanistic framework for FtsW substrate recognition and functional activation, highlighting tractable sites for structure- and mechanism-based antibiotic discovery targeting SEDS-class cell wall synthases.

title: A Three-Axis Framework for Therapy Prioritization in MBD4-Deficient Tumors: De-confounded Synthetic Lethality Modeling, Replication-Stress Pharmacology, and PARP1 Trapping Decoupling
summary: Background: Loss-of-function mutations in MBD4 (methyl-CpG-binding domain protein 4) cause a specialized base excision repair (BER) deficiency characterized by hypermutated CpG>TpG signatures and sensitivity to immune checkpoint blockade. However, post-immunotherapy treatment prioritization remains empirically unmapped. In clinical oncology, DNA damage response (DDR) defects are frequently extrapolated to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor (PARPi) sensitivity by analogy to homologous recombination deficiency (HRD), without testing whether upstream glycosylase loss generates the nicked single-strand break (SSB) intermediates required for toxic PARP1-DNA trapping. Methods: We developed a three-axis framework integrating mechanistic curation, large-scale pharmacogenomics (DepMap 24Q2 CRISPR/RNA-seq, n=1,517; GDSC2 dose-response profiling, n=928; PRISM Repurposing), and a 5-Layer De-confounded Synthetic Lethality Machine Learning (SL-ML) Engine (SL-XGBRanker). To prevent functional dilution from variants of uncertain significance, MBD4 loss-of-function (MBD4-LOF) was strictly restricted to truncating and canonical splice-site alleles (21 of 36 mutated lines), independently validated by nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD; two-sided p2s = 0.0367), while excluding 15 lines harboring 19 non-truncating variants (18 missense, 1 inframe deletion). All primary pharmacogenomic comparisons were evaluated using two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests (p2s), bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs), Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) multiplicity correction across six pre-specified candidate axes, and Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) for expression equivalence. Results: Our analysis delineates three distinct therapeutic axes in MBD4-LOF tumors: (1) Cytidine Analog Vulnerability (Axis 1): Mechanistic structural evidence demonstrates that MBD4 loss impairs excision of 5-substituted pyrimidine analogs and deaminated bases, creating a direct biochemical bottleneck to gemcitabine and 5-fluorouracil incorporation. (2) ATR-Check1 Replication-Stress Vulnerability (Axis 2): In GDSC2 profiling, MBD4-LOF cell lines exhibit significant sensitivity to the ATR inhibitor ceralasertib (AZD6738). In the clinically relevant TP53-mutant background-which disables the G1/S checkpoint and forces reliance on ATR-mediated S/G2 arrest-MBD4-LOF lines (n=11 vs n=619 WT) demonstrate pronounced ceralasertib hypersensitivity (Delta LN_IC50 = -1.07, 95% CI [-1.62, -0.41], Cohen's d = -0.74, p2s = 0.0060, BH-FDR q = 0.036; Delta AUC = -0.087, d = -0.89, p2s = 0.0017), with 11/11 leave-one-out (LOO) jackknife iterations retaining two-sided significance (p2s <= 0.014). This genotype-associated dependency remains robust in the unstratified pan-cancer cohort (n=14 vs n=914 WT; Delta LN_IC50 = -0.73, 95% CI [-1.31, -0.11], d = -0.50, p2s = 0.0430; Delta AUC = -0.056, d = -0.56, p2s = 0.0259) and after purging microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) lines (n=10 vs n=906 WT MSS; Delta LN_IC50 = -0.91, 95% CI [-1.50, -0.22], d = -0.62, p2s = 0.0307). By contrast, Wee1 inhibition (adavosertib; n=15 vs n=920 WT; Delta LN_IC50 = -0.35, p2s = 0.1667) does not reach statistical significance. (3) Absence of Single-Agent PARPi Sensitivity (Axis 3): While PARP1 transcript abundance strongly governs pan-cancer PARPi cytotoxicity across n=481 cell lines (rho = -0.416, p < 10^-21 across five clinical PARPi), MBD4-LOF tumors (n=19 vs n=1,498 WT) show zero compensatory PARP1 upregulation (median 6.77 vs 6.66 log2[TPM+1], Delta median = +0.11, 95% CI [-0.39, +0.71], p2s = 0.605; TOST equivalence p_TOST = 0.0199 within +/- 0.50 log2[TPM+1]). Direct GDSC2 evaluation of MBD4-LOF (n=8) versus WT (n=478) confirms complete absence of single-agent PARPi sensitization across talazoparib (p2s = 0.973), olaparib (p2s = 0.522), niraparib (p2s = 0.877), rucaparib (p2s = 0.804), veliparib (p2s = 0.538), and the composite 5-drug mean PARPi Z-score (Delta median Z = -0.024, 95% CI [-0.84, +0.60], p2s = 0.841). Under Leave-One-Anchor-Out cross-validation across 12 canonical DDR genes (370 gene-drug pairs), our 5-Layer De-confounded SL-ML Engine achieves an out-of-fold AUROC of 0.9716, AUPRC of 0.8007, and Top-1 accuracy of 82.86%, zero-shot ranking gemcitabine (#1) and ceralasertib (#2) as the top therapeutic dependencies for held-out MBD4 while rejecting all PARP inhibitors (ranks #13, #27, #28, #31). Conclusion: MBD4-LOF tumors exhibit a selective, TP53-potentiated pharmacological dependency on ATR kinase inhibition alongside mechanistic vulnerability to cytidine analogs, but lack both the nicked BER repair intermediates and the PARP1 target expression required for single-agent PARP inhibitor efficacy.

title: Deep Learning Identifies BMI-Associated Morphologic Features in Breast Cancer Tissue
summary: Multiple epidemiological studies have established obesity as an adverse factor in breast cancer incidence, progression, and clinical outcomes. However, the biological mechanisms underlying these associations remain incompletely understood. In peritumoral adipose tissue, obesity is associated with chronic inflammation, macrophage recruitment, and broader alterations in the local microenvironment. Whether these obesity-associated changes are accompanied by distinct morphologic features within the tumor and non-adipose stromal compartments remains unclear. In this study, we investigated whether an AI-based pathology foundation model could support the development of machine learning algorithms capable of identifying obesity-associated morphologic patterns in histopathology images, with a particular focus on tumor and stromal regions. In a cohort of 195 patients with breast cancer, machine learning models using vector embeddings from non-adipose stromal regions classified high BMI ([≥]30 kg/m2) versus low BMI (<25 kg/m2) with an average AUC of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.73-0.83), consistently outperforming models based on tumor-only or combined tumor-stroma regions. These obesity-associated stromal signatures were observed across subgroups defined by hormone-receptor status and age, indicating that they are not restricted to specific clinical populations. Complementary embedding-based dissimilarity analysis further showed that higher BMI was associated with reduced inter-patient heterogeneity in both tumor and stromal tissues. Overall, these findings suggest that obesity is associated with distinct morphologic alterations in both tumor and non-adipose stromal tissues. Notably, the stromal compartment emerged as a particularly informative indicator of obesity-associated morphology and demonstrated reduced inter-patient heterogeneity among individuals with high BMI.

title: Methylene blue modulates G3BP1-associated condensation and attenuates Kras-driven pancreatic preneoplastic lesions
summary: Abstract Stress granules (SGs) are dynamic biomolecular condensates implicated in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), with G3BP1/2 serving as key regulators of their assembly. We combined structure-based screening of FDA-approved drugs with cellular and biochemical assays and identified methylene blue (MB) as a modulator of SG assembly. MB suppressed SG accumulation across multiple PDAC cell lines under arsenite (AS)-induced stress, nutrient deprivation, and heat shock without reducing the abundance of major SG-associated proteins. In reconstituted systems, MB inhibited G3BP1 condensation with or without added RNA and showed a nonsignificant trend toward lower G3BP1-Caprin1 co-immunoprecipitation in cells. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations predicted a potential MB interaction site within the G3BP1 NTF2-like (NTF2L) domain. The G3BP1 V11A/F15A/F33A/F124A mutant retained basal condensate-forming capacity but showed reduced responsiveness to MB compared with wild-type G3BP1, implicating this region in MB-mediated regulation. In Kras-driven KC mice, chronic oral MB administration was associated with reduced pancreatic G3BP1-positive puncta, increased acinar preservation, and decreased preneoplastic lesion burden, epithelial proliferation, and stromal remodeling, without overt abnormalities in the evaluated endpoints. Together, these findings identify MB as a small-molecule probe that modulates G3BP1 condensation dynamics and demonstrate that chronic MB treatment is associated with the attenuation of early Kras driven pancreatic preneoplastic lesion progression in vivo.
